Subject: Mathematics
Concept/Based On: Example 1 — grouped-data Pearson coefficient, variation 1
Question: A grouped distribution has class intervals 12-22, 22-32, 32-42, 42-52, 52-62 with frequencies [9, 17, 29, 14, 6]. Using class marks and u=(xᵢ−37)/10, find Karl Pearson’s coefficient of skewness.
Hint: Find the class marks, use the assumed-mean u values to obtain the mean and S.D., then find the modal class and apply (Mean−Mode)/S.D.
Explanation: Take class marks 17, 27, 37, 47, 57 and let a=37, h=10. Then Σfu=-9, Σfu²=91, N=75, so ū=-0.12. Mean = a+hū = 35.8. Variance = h²[Σfu²/N−ū²] = 119.8933, hence S.D.=10.9496. The modal class has fₘ=29, f₁=17, f₂=14, so Mode = L+(fₘ−f₁)h/(2fₘ−f₁−f₂) = 36.4444. Thus Skₚ=(Mean−Mode)/S.D.=-0.0589. The option B comes from reversing the sign (Mode−Mean). The option C comes from dividing by variance instead of S.D. The option D comes from omitting f₂ in the modal-mode denominator.

Concept/Based On: Example 2 — grouped quartiles and Bowley coefficient, variation 1
Question: A grouped wage distribution has class intervals 0-50, 50-100, 100-150, 150-200, 200-250, 250-300 with frequencies [5, 12, 28, 31, 17, 7]. Find Bowley’s coefficient of skewness.
Hint: Locate N/4, N/2 and 3N/4 observations, calculate Q₁, Q₂ and Q₃ from their classes, then use Bowley’s formula.
Explanation: N=100. Q1: position 25, class 100-150, f=28, C.F.=17, Q1=114.2857; Q2: position 50, class 150-200, f=31, C.F.=45, Q2=158.0645; Q3: position 75, class 150-200, f=31, C.F.=45, Q3=198.3871. Using Q=L+h[(position−C.F. previous)/f], the quartiles are Q₁=114.2857, Q₂=158.0645, Q₃=198.3871. Therefore Skᵦ=(Q₃+Q₁−2Q₂)/(Q₃−Q₁)=-0.0411. The option A comes from omitting 2Q₂ in the numerator. The option C comes from using Q₃−Q₁ itself as the numerator. The option D comes from using an incorrect median position (N/2+1), which changes Q₂.

Question: For a skewed distribution, Mean=80, Median=77 and S.D.=6. Find the Mode and Karl Pearson’s coefficient of skewness.
Hint: First use Mean−Mode=3(Mean−Median) to obtain the mode; then substitute mean, mode and S.D. in Pearson’s formula.
Explanation: Use Mean−Mode=3(Mean−Median). Hence 80−Mode=3(80−77)=9, so Mode=71. Then Skₚ=(Mean−Mode)/S.D.=(80−71)/6=1.5. The option A comes from adding 3(Mean−Median) instead of subtracting it when finding Mode. The option B comes from using Median in place of Mode in Pearson’s formula. The option D comes from dividing by the variance (S.D.²) instead of S.D.
